work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: “Evil is not a substance, but a way of behaving that comes solely from the will.”
“Those who have brought the sickness of their conduct upon themselves by their own will.”
“This way of behaving, which arises as something added, can very easily be separated from the will of those who are sick.”

“If evil had arisen in such a way that it could no longer be removed from the will—that is, if, although it was something added, it had been added in a way that made it impossible ever to separate it from the will—one could rightly say that evil was not a substance, but that the substance itself could no longer exist without the evil added to it. But if evil was added, and the starting point of its addition was the will rather than the substance, evil can easily be separated from the substance. Then the substance subject to the will can be kept completely pure, so that not even any traces of evil remain.”
translator_notes: Augustine identifies these as passages from Basil used in Book 4 of Julian’s To Turbantius. They are Basil’s words as Julian quoted them, preserved in separated excerpts, with Augustine’s replies removed. The source identifies Basil, That God Is Not the Author of Evils, 5. “Substance” means the underlying thing or nature; “something added” means a condition it acquired, rather than something belonging to its essence.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: “If chastity is a virtue, but the body were evil in its very substance, it would be impossible to find a chaste body. A body belonging to shameful conduct could not become a body belonging to virtue. But when it is made holy, it becomes a body of virtue. Thus virtue shares in the body, and the body in virtue; through virtue it also becomes God’s temple (1 Corinthians 6:19). If every body belonged to sexual immorality, it would certainly be impossible to find chastity in bodies. Only then could we count evil as belonging to the very nature of bodies. But if the body has attained such worth, has been adorned with so much honor, and has put on such a garment of purity that it deserves to be its Maker’s house and becomes the bridal chamber of God’s Son—so that the Father and the Son are pleased to come and choose bodies as their dwelling (John 14:23)—how can the Manichaean claim fail to be exposed as detestable and absurd?”
translator_notes: Basil’s argument is quoted by Julian, rather than newly composed by him. The two Bible references mark clear allusions in this quotation; the other Bible passages in Augustine’s response are not included.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Saint John of Constantinople denies that there is original sin in infants. In the homily he gave about those who had been baptized, he says:

“Blessed is God, who alone has done wonders (Psalm 72:18), who made everything and transforms everything. Look: those who were captives a little while ago now enjoy the peace of freedom. Those who wandered as strangers are now citizens of the church (Ephesians 2:19). Those who were in the confusion of sin now share in righteousness. They are not only free, but holy; not only holy, but righteous; not only righteous, but sons; not only sons, but heirs; not only heirs, but Christ’s brothers; not only Christ’s brothers, but fellow heirs (Romans 8:15–17); not only fellow heirs, but members of his body (1 Corinthians 12:27); not only members, but a temple (1 Corinthians 6:19); not only a temple, but instruments of the Spirit.

“You see how many gifts baptism gives. Some people think that heavenly grace consists only in the forgiveness of sins. We, however, have counted ten honors. This is why we baptize infants too, although they are not stained by sin: so that holiness, righteousness, adoption, inheritance, and brotherhood with Christ may be added to them, and so that they may be his members.”
translator_notes: Julian introduces and quotes John Chrysostom’s Homily to the Newly Baptized near the end of To Turbantius, Book 4. Augustine disputes Julian’s reading in the next section: the Greek says that infants “have no sins,” which Augustine takes to mean personal sins. The translation preserves the form Julian quoted rather than silently substituting Augustine’s correction. Psalm 72:18 is Psalm 71:18 in the Latin/Greek numbering. The other Bible references identify clear allusions, not formal verse citations supplied by Julian.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Since it is plainly clear that this is the sound and true position, supported first by reason and then by the authority of Scripture, and always upheld by the learning of holy men—who did not give truth its authority by agreeing with it, but received a good testimony and glory from sharing in it—let no prudent person be disturbed by a conspiracy of the lost.
translator_notes: “A conspiracy of the lost” is Julian’s polemical description of his opponents, repeated by Augustine at 1.7.30. “Lost” here means spiritually ruined people.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: One man has come forward who wants people to think that the whole battle depends on him.
translator_notes: Augustine identifies himself as the man Julian means.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [You oppose us with] only the crowd’s murmuring.
translator_notes: The surviving quoted words are fitted into Augustine’s own first-person sentence. The bracketed opening supplies the change of speaker needed to make Julian’s accusation intelligible.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [This position] cannot find a defender among so large a multitude.
translator_notes: The bracketed words identify the disputed teaching without treating Augustine’s surrounding explanation as Julian’s own wording.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Since, according to the Gospel’s judgment, a tree should be recognized by its fruits (Matthew 7:16–18), should this man be listened to when he says that marriage is good, yet declares that nothing but evil comes from it?
translator_notes: The Gospel wording also has a parallel in Luke 6:43–44. The hypothetical reply Augustine supplies later in this section is not presented as a surviving quotation from Julian.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Evil things cannot come from good things.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Sin cannot be transmitted through nature, because the devil’s work is not allowed to pass through God’s work.
translator_notes: Augustine repeats abbreviated forms of this claim in the same section and at 1.9.44.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Original sin has disappeared, because the root of evil cannot be placed in what you call a gift of God.
translator_notes: Julian means that his argument has disposed of the doctrine of original sin. Augustine repeats the claim about the root of evil several times here and at 1.9.44.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The nature of things does not allow evil to be brought forth from good, or anything unjust from what is just.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: That from which, and through which, bad fruit has appeared must itself be evil.
translator_notes: This continues the argument from the tree and its fruit in Matthew 7:16–18. The other quotations from Julian in this section repeat the preceding fragments.
